tail.summary: Grounded in formative interviews with 9 fiction writers, VeriForge divides cognitive labour so the system owns domain discovery while the author keeps full initiative over narrative synthesis -- a response to tools that demand queries authors cannot formulate or generate finished prose that homogenises voice. Three mechanisms: proactive inline highlighting that flags knowledge gaps while drafting, dual-stream querying pairing conversational answers with source-anchored Knowledge Cards, and a spatial Knowledge Canvas for organising discovered material. Backed by graph-based RAG over domain sources and evaluated in a within-subjects study (N=12).

tail.title: Private Etymology: Designing Relational Reuse of Shared Symbols in Long-Term Human-AI Interaction
tail.summary: Proposes a machine-representable relational provenance recording how a dyad-specific expression -- a personal idiom, inside joke or negotiated shorthand -- is proposed, interpreted, negotiated, repaired, reused, revised, stabilized, contested, forgotten or retired over time, plus 'relational reuse' for reactivating it later without re-explaining. Contributes a lifecycle model, a machine-readable schema and a working Apple Watch prototype in which a language model classifies discrete conversational evidence while deterministic local code decides whether a Shared Symbol may update, deliberately keeping a free-form model confidence score out of the loop.

tail.title: Decoding-Level Taboo: A Diagnostic Stress Test for LLM Robustness
tail.summary: A zero-prompt diagnostic that intervenes directly in logit space at runtime, dynamically masking primary candidate tokens at word boundaries to force machine circumlocution and push models off the narrow, highly optimised generation corridor that benchmarks reward. Across several open-weight families, off-path robustness improves with both parameter scale and post-training instruction alignment. The authors pitch it as a reusable primitive for synthetic dataset generation, runtime guardrail stress-testing and pre-deployment reliability auditing.

tail.title: Pragmatic Attack Surface: Vulnerabilities of Implicit Context in Large Language Models
tail.summary: Existing jailbreaks exploit explicit linguistic cues in prompts and are largely handled by safety alignment. This paper targets the implicit pragmatic context -- world knowledge and social norms needed to interpret language but never stated in it -- arguing safety alignment underuses it, creating a mismatch between how humans interpret language and how alignment is trained. Exploiting that mismatch yields high attack success rates, substantially outperforming baseline attacks across open- and closed-source models.

tail.title: Not an A11y: How Android Accessibility Exposes Mobile AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
tail.summary: Mobile agent frameworks read the Android accessibility tree as their primary interface representation, and that unsanitized metadata is a systemic indirect-prompt-injection channel. Adversarial prompts make agents abandon their objectives, cross context boundaries and take unauthorized device actions, demonstrated in both visually hidden and fully exposed scenarios. MobileRun with Gemma4:31B reaches an attack success rate of 0.822 while Mobile-Use with Qwen3.6:35B cuts it to 0.150 without eliminating context drift or unauthorized actions.

tail.title: Quantization Degradation in Large Language Models: A Signal-Noise Perspective
tail.summary: Systematic weight-only post-training quantization study across bit-widths, methods, model scales and tasks on multiple families: 4-bit usually preserves performance, 2-bit causes broad degradation, and 3-bit degradation is real but varies sharply with task type, method and scale. A signal-to-noise decomposition attributes newly introduced error to weight-error magnitude, task-specific signal strength, and how strongly quantization error aligns with task-specific activations. Cross-layer propagation analysis shows errors can be attenuated, preserved or amplified across layers, with larger models benefiting from weaker amplification.

tail.title: Tied Trit-Planes: Constraining PTQTP to a Uniform Nine-Level Quantizer, with a Persistent Folded Format for Disk-Streamed Mixture-of-Experts Serving
tail.summary: Tying PTQTP's two per-group scales to a fixed ratio of three collapses its two-ternary-plane decomposition into a single uniform nine-level quantizer, which folds losslessly into one 4-bit code plane used as the persistent serving representation at 4.0625 bits/weight. Applied one-shot to the routed experts of the 284B-A13B DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 from released MXFP4 weights, streaming experts from SSD on a 64 GB laptop. Against a 4.5-bit Q4_K baseline it matches the official serving API on 5/5 fixtures at step 0 (Q4_K: 4/5), scores 86 vs 84 on a 100-item MMLU subset, decodes 6.7% faster and ships 9% smaller files.

tail.title: Motif 3: Technical Report
tail.summary: A decoder-only Mixture-of-Experts model with 314B total parameters and 13.2B activated per token, using 384 routed experts per sparse layer with eight selected. The architecture centres on Grouped Differential Latent Attention, combining grouped differential attention with Multi-head Latent Attention's compressed KV representation, plus manifold-constrained hyper-connections, Expert-Specific PolyNorm activations and multi-token prediction. Pretrained on ~12.5T tokens with selective MXFP8 compute and window-aware context parallelism up to 256K context; post-training combines general SFT, six RL-trained specialist teachers and multi-teacher on-policy distillation.

tail.title: Matryoshka Language Model Suites
tail.summary: Instead of training and serving each model in a suite separately, this stacks sub-models of increasing size into a single nested architecture trained end to end, cutting total suite parameters, enabling low-cost distillation from largest to all smaller sub-models at every step, and making the speculative-decoding draft model a subset of the verifier. A 500M/1.5B/3B suite matches independently trained baselines on benchmarks and on validation and out-of-domain perplexity while using 36% less training compute and improving speculative-decoding throughput by 14-26%.

tail.title: The Evolution of Mixture-of-Experts Architectures in Large Language Models: Routing, Topology, Load Balancing, and Expert Parallelism
tail.summary: Technical survey organising modern MoE systems along five coupled dimensions -- expert granularity, expert topology, routing freedom, scope of load balancing, and execution structure -- and presenting eight architectural milestones as a dependency graph with six mainline developments and two orthogonal branches rather than as successive generations. Individual systems are analysed through four control planes (Expert Topology, Routing, Balance, Expert Parallelism) that connect Top-k routing, shared and fine-grained experts and dynamic composition to token dispatch, device placement and all-to-all communication. Closes with equal-budget pretraining experiments and open questions.

tail.title: Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP): Hallucination Detection in LLMs from Hidden States
tail.summary: Extends standard linear probing for answer-level hallucination detection by augmenting the input to a frozen LLM with a small number of learnable prompt embeddings, keeping the backbone frozen and adding few trainable parameters. Evaluated on TriviaQA, GSM8K and MedQA with Qwen3 models at multiple scales, PEP beats standard linear probes in the main in-distribution setting and remains effective for pre-generation prediction and cross-model transfer. Robust cross-dataset transfer remains the open failure.

tail.title: RAVEN-Eval: Rubric-Guided Automatic Evaluation for AI Video Generation Models Based on LMM Preference Judgement
tail.summary: An LMM-as-a-judge framework for video generation built on 150 text-to-video and 100 image-to-video tasks with over 4,500 collected generations, where judges make pairwise comparisons against task-specific rubrics rather than generic fidelity criteria. An anchor-based model insertion scheme keeps the cost of adding new models down. They evaluate 20 video generation models AND the judging capability of 13 LMM judges, publishing both as leaderboards.

tail.title: Do Evaluation Metrics Detect Errors in Classical Chinese to English Translations?
tail.summary: Tests whether automatic MT metrics developed for modern languages remain reliable for historical translation, using Classical Chinese to English. The diagnostic framework builds minimal pairs capturing error types that actually matter in scholarly use, probing both reference-based and reference-free metrics for error sensitivity and for tolerance of valid variation. Every metric shows blind spots, with MetricX24 best overall.

tail.title: LLM Reasoning for Subjective Tasks: Failure Modes, Mitigation, and Dynamic Reasoning Routing
tail.summary: Large-scale study across proprietary and open-source models on four real verification tasks from a production recommender, asking whether explicit reasoning generalises from objective math to subjective human-centric rubrics. Rigid math-centric reasoning traces actively degrade verification, and standard RLVR triggers 'reasoning collapse' where the policy abandons deliberation for rapid heuristic guessing; a conditional length-penalized post-training algorithm halts it. The sharpest result: across 1,500 synthesized personas, verification accuracy swings by nearly 0.38 macro-F1 purely on the socio-linguistic framing of the reasoning persona.

tail.title: From Values to Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models for Governmental Use in Dutch
tail.summary: Developed with a major Dutch municipal organisation through an advisory board, user research and a survey of civil-servant chatbot users, the 'Grip on LLMs' framework operationalises six dimensions -- factuality, honesty, social bias, energy consumption, cost and training-data transparency -- into a suite covering 30+ multilingual and Dutch-specific models. No model excels across all dimensions and the trade-offs are structural: higher quality always costs more environmentally and financially, while bias is largely independent of both. Factuality and honesty turn out to be governed by distinct properties, so answering correctly does not predict admitting ignorance.

tail.title: Qualifying and Quantifying Risk under the EU AI Act
tail.summary: Addresses the tension in the AI Act between a definition of risk (probability combined with severity) that implies quantification and a focus on fundamental rights that is typically qualitative. The proposed two-step framework balances protection of fundamental rights against legitimate provider and deployer purposes and the burden of regulatory measures, and the authors argue the Act implies a 'severity-first' analysis in which harm severity is weighed before probability. They close on the risk of 'risk hacking' if quantification is left to providers and deployers.

tail.title: Yesterday's Shield, Today's Spear: A Self-Evolving Safety Guardrail in Production
tail.summary: A multi-agent system running in production that monitors live traffic behind a deployed guardrail and surfaces two failure classes -- jailbreaks novel in form and harmful categories novel in content -- then synthesizes targeted paired training data, rebalances the batch toward the direction the model errs in, and routes the training action to the diagnosed gap. Over six rounds of live evolution a 1.7B guardrail adapts to a new threat in 16-24 hours with about two hours of human effort, against 40-90 hours for the manual process. In production since April 2026 it autonomously closed 14 of 15 new threat scenarios in two months.

tail.title: Multi-Agent AI Safety as an Institutional Design Problem
tail.summary: A frozen 5,280-episode study suite asking which parts of an AI institution actually produce safety, spanning four model families in the pre-specified delegation experiment plus three more endpoints in a high-conflict diagnostic. A detailed constitutional prompt and a provenance-aware executable guard each produced 0/384 realized violations, though the guard blocked prohibited attempts in 51/384 episodes of which 44 later completed safely. The decisive contrast is in laundering scenarios, where a local-state guard admitted violations in 22/96 episodes against 0/96 for provenance enforcement (p = 4.77e-7).

tail.title: Build it, Break it, Repeat: Benchmarking and improving LLM-manipulated disinformation detection in social media posts
tail.summary: Adapts Build it, Break it, Fix it into iterative adversarial sessions that stress-test disinformation detectors under deliberate evasion, on the grounds that static held-out benchmarks say nothing about behaviour under transformation. Over five iterations the strongest breaker combined back-translation with LLM persona-based rewriting, hitting a 95% label-flip rate while preserving meaning. The best builder, a triplet contrastive model with dynamic anchor switching, averaged 72.68% accuracy, 15 points above a fine-tuned e5-small-LoRA baseline on the most robust adversarial set.

tail.title: Fairness in Link Prediction Beyond Demographic Parity: A Reproducibility Study
tail.summary: Reproduces the claim that demographic parity fails to detect exposure bias in ranked link prediction because it ignores WHERE links appear in the ranking, confirming that parity can look satisfied while some subgroup-pair links are systematically ranked lower. The rank-aware Normalized Discounted KL-divergence does detect those disparities, and the MORAL post-processing method reproduces as improving exposure fairness at competitive utility. Robustness is extended with synthetic homophily settings, categorical sensitive attributes and a subgroup-pair-adapted Attention-Weighted Rank Fairness metric, with a corrected implementation released.

tail.title: Mitigating Over-Personalization in LLMs via Structured Memory
tail.summary: Studies two failure modes of persistent long-term memory: cross-domain leakage, where memories from one life domain contaminate responses in another, and memory-induced sycophancy, where stored user beliefs make the model agree rather than answer truthfully. The intervention is inference-time only, changing how memories are presented without touching model or memory contents. Across seven models on PersistBench, partitioning memories by domain instead of injecting them as an unstructured list cuts leakage by 8.8% on average while preserving utility.

tail.title: DSLE: A Learning Environment for Dark Souls Boss Encounters
tail.summary: A containerized Gymnasium-style benchmark exposing all 22 boss encounters of Dark Souls: Remastered, with real-time combat, high-dimensional visual input and sparse terminal rewards, each step a real action against the running game. On the five-boss DSLE-5 subset, an expert system and an evolutionary baseline beat only the tutorial boss (63% and 43% peak win rates) while PPO and DQN trained from vision show no measurable learning -- at most 0.33% on the tutorial boss and 0% elsewhere, at tens of wall-clock hours per run. Running the evolutionary baseline across all 22 encounters with level-50 stats still leaves most bosses unwon.

tail.title: A Machine Learning Based Search for Lunar Anomalies
tail.summary: Tests a Beta-Variational Autoencoder as an unsupervised anomaly detector over Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Narrow Angle Camera imagery at roughly 0.5-2 metres per pixel, collected since 2009. The model is asked to surface both geologic features of interest -- rockfall deposits, fresh impact craters, irregular mare patches, volcanic pits and collapsed lava tubes -- and artificial objects such as landed spacecraft. It recovered Plaskett Crater and Paracelsus C Crater plus numerous landed technological assets at a statistically significant rate.

tail.title: Imaginative Generative AI: Crossing the Entropy Wall into Worlds Beyond Imitation
tail.summary: Generative models target the data distribution, an objective that neither repairs diversity a generator has lost nor says how generation should extend past the data's own diversity. IGA makes diversity part of target-distribution design, selecting among distributions close to a reference one whose spectral diversity -- von Neumann entropy of the kernel covariance operator in a fixed representation space -- hits a prescribed level. The spectral entropy of the population data distribution defines an 'Entropy Wall': below it the method does diversity repair, above it the data distribution becomes infeasible and the model deliberately departs from it, giving one regularization path from imitation to imagination.

tail.title: Agentic Auto-Research is Fuzz Testing
tail.summary: Argues the dominant generate-and-rank paradigm for autonomous research agents misses the sparse-feedback problem, and that within a declared research problem an agent is running a greybox fuzzer's control loop: propose, execute, observe, choose what to try next. Fuzzers rarely find a bug but coverage makes partial progress observable on every execution and directs the next mutation, rather than only ranking finished runs. The position is that each experiment should expose a cheap dense signal of epistemic progress that steers the next intervention, with final validation kept on evidence protected from adaptive reuse.

tail.title: Spectral Outliers Reveal Dominant Learned Structure in Transformer Attention
tail.summary: Applies Marchenko-Pastur random matrix theory to separate each pre-trained attention projection matrix into a random-like bulk and a set of spectral outliers, then validates the split causally: zeroing the identified outliers in Mistral-7B drives HellaSwag, MMLU and PIQA near random chance, while zeroing a count-matched subset of bulk singular values degrades performance far less. Across 11 pre-trained transformers five patterns recur, including that Q projections carry the most outliers, that V projections under grouped-query attention lack clean signal/noise separation, and that specific residual-stream dimensions persist as band outliers across layers in K and O.

tail.title: Abstracted Away: Resisting Alienation and Ungrounded Abstraction in AI Research Communities
tail.summary: Three early-career critical AI researchers use autoethnography to argue that abstraction operates in computational AI research not only as a technical practice but as a social norm that creates distance from material realities -- separating standards of legitimacy from lived experience of harm, misaligning stated goals from operationalising practices, and letting career demands crowd out reflection. Three vignettes narrate encountering and resisting this alienation, including having aspects of their backgrounds overlooked and others tokenized. They build an interpretive framework of alienation's preconditions, mechanisms and harms, identifying 'affect abstraction' as the high-leverage mechanism.

tail.title: NVIDIA launches Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B — an open Mamba2-Transformer hybrid MoE for the agent execution layer
tail.summary: NVIDIA gave a coordinated public launch to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a 33B-parameter (NVIDIA markets it as 30B) mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters, pitched not as a frontier reasoner but as the cheap execution layer under a smarter planner: tool calls, result validation, subagent delegation. It landed simultaneously on Ollama v0.32.9, OpenRouter at $0.10/$0.25 per M with a free 1M-context tier, and as ggml-org and bartowski GGUFs, under the OpenMDW 1.1 licence. Worth noting for provenance: the BF16 and NVFP4 weights had actually been sitting on Hugging Face since 1-5 August, so this is a launch of attention, not of artefacts, and the 'built for your own hardware' framing collides with the file sizes below.

tail.title: CyberStrike-OffSec-35B gets abliterated within a day — refusal removal on a purpose-built offensive-security model
tail.summary: huihui-ai applied refusal ablation to oyildirim/CyberStrike-OffSec-35B, a Qwen3.5-MoE pentesting and tool-calling fine-tune, using the remove-refusals-with-transformers method the card itself describes as 'a crude, proof-of-concept implementation'. This is a different case from the usual abliteration of a general assistant: the base model was already trained toward offensive-security capability, so the ablation removes the last layer of restraint from something purpose-built, which makes it a cleaner test case for what suppression removal actually buys versus what the fine-tune already provided. On VRAM it does not reach you: the GGUF repo publishes only bf16 71.07GB, Q8_0 37.80GB and Q4_K 21.71GB plus a 0.90GB mmproj, with no sub-Q4 rung.

tail.title: Abacus.AI revives the Smaug line as an agentic fine-tune of Kimi K3's 2.8T MoE
tail.summary: Smaug-Agentic is a supervised multi-turn agentic fine-tune of Moonshot's 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3, continuing the line from Smaug-72B-v0.1, and the card is unusually disciplined about scope: it states the fine-tune adapts behaviour only, leaves every architectural parameter unchanged, and therefore serves on any stack that already serves K3. The weights are real — 94 safetensors shards totalling roughly 1.56TB across 111 files — which also means this is firmly a rented-cluster model, not a local one. It is worth watching as a controlled comparison point, since a behaviour-only fine-tune on an unchanged frontier base is a cleaner ablation than most 'agentic' releases offer.

tail.title: Upstage ships Solar Pro 4 as a closed model — 524K context at $0.03/$0.12 per million tokens
tail.summary: Upstage announced Solar Pro 4 on 11 August as 'the agentic model that finishes the job' and it appeared on OpenRouter a day earlier with a 524,288-token context at $0.03 input and $0.12 output per million. There are no open weights: both upstage/solar-pro4 and upstage/Solar-Pro-4 return 401 on the Hugging Face API, which is a break from the Solar Open 2 sovereign-model line Upstage published in July. At that price it is roughly 10x cheaper than Qwen3.5-397B on input, which makes it worth a cheap side-by-side on a judging task before believing either the pricing or the agentic claim.

tail.title: Sakana AI opens a Japanese-specialised reasoning API, Namazu, built on Kimi K2.6
tail.summary: Sakana Namazu is a Japanese-language reasoning model built on Kimi K2.6 with additional training for Japanese instruction following and business contexts, now live on OpenRouter at $0.95/$4.00 per M with 262K context. It is a clean instance of the sovereign-language-model pattern: take a Chinese open-weight frontier base, continue-train for a national language and market, sell it as an API rather than weights. For cross-lingual bias work the interesting question is whether the demographic behaviour of the K2.6 base survives the Japanese continuation or gets reshaped by it, which is testable given both are addressable through the same router.

tail.title: Anthropic's Compliance API now returns transcripts of Claude Code sessions running on employee machines
tail.summary: As of 11 August, Claude Enterprise organisations can retrieve full transcripts of locally-run Cowork and Claude Code sessions through three new Compliance API endpoints, using an existing Compliance Access Key with the read:compliance_user_data scope. This extends a capability that on 3 August only covered remote claude.ai sessions to sessions executing on a user's own machine. If you ever run Claude Code under a client's enterprise org rather than your personal subscription, the boundary of what is retrievable by that org has just moved, and it is worth knowing before a consulting engagement rather than after.

tail.title: BananaMind-2-SLMoE tests sequence-level expert routing at 25M parameters and says plainly that it is not a product
tail.summary: A 25.45M-total-parameter MoE that picks one fixed set of 13 experts from 64 by reading the first 32 tokens, then reuses that route for every token in the message and response — 7.9M active parameters per message, 8 layers, 4,096 context, 8,192 vocab, 110MB of weights. The card is refreshingly honest: it states this is a research checkpoint to test whether sequence-level routing works at this scale at all, that a V2 is planned with routing and expert-balance fixes, and it publishes no benchmark claims. The motivating idea is the one that matters for a 16GB card — a hypothetical 744B-total model with E30B active could keep inactive experts on disk and load only the selected route — so this is the seed of an approach worth tracking even though the artefact itself does nothing useful.

tail.title: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning's explainability card declares it a Mamba2-Transformer hybrid
tail.summary: The explainability field-card lists the model type as 'Text-to-text Mamba2-Transformer Hybrid', which is the architectural fact the launch blog and the Ollama post both omit, and it is the most likely explanation for why the GGUF quant ladder is flat from 2 to 4 bits. It also discloses that synthetic training data was filtered by a Gemma-3 4B model fine-tuned on NVIDIA's Aegis content-safety dataset — a distillation-and-filtering chain worth noting when you are reasoning about where a model's demographic priors came from. The card's 'describe how the model works' answer is the generic next-token boilerplate, which is a good illustration of structured disclosure fields being filled without disclosing anything.

tail.title: Arize Phoenix v20.0.0 lands agent session persistence and trace-annotation filtering in the span DSL
tail.summary: Phoenix cut a major version adding agent session persistence and support for trace_annotations in the span filter DSL, on top of v19.20/19.21 the previous day which added dataset-split REST endpoints and experiment tags. Annotation-aware span filtering is the piece that matters for a judge pipeline: it lets you slice traces by the annotation an evaluator attached rather than by raw span attributes, which is how you isolate the disagreement cases in an IRR pass. Note the paired client v3.0.0 is a breaking release.

tail.title: openai-agents-python v0.20.0 silently changes the default model to gpt-5.6-luna
tail.summary: The release notes are explicit that v0.20.0 is minor only in version number: it changes the implicit default model to gpt-5.6-luna and migrates the MCP dependency in a way that can break applications with customised local HTTP transports. Explicit model arguments, run-level overrides and OPENAI_DEFAULT_MODEL still win, so the exposure is code that never named a model. This is the classic silent-drift failure mode for evaluation work — an unpinned default changing under you invalidates cross-run comparability without any error surfacing.

tail.title: vLLM v0.27.1 patches quantized DSpark Markov heads, days after a 561-commit v0.27.0
tail.summary: v0.27.1 is a single-item patch on top of v0.27.0 adding support for quantized DSpark Markov heads. The context is that v0.27.0, which appeared with an empty body when it was tagged on 10 August, has since been filled in with full notes: 561 commits from 242 contributors, headlined by a complete Kimi K3 stack — core model files and kernels landing in one release. If you are pinning a serving version for a reproducible eval run, 0.27.1 is the one that actually serves quantized speculative heads correctly.

tail.title: Ollama v0.32.9 adds the Nemotron 3 architecture and a Muse Glimmer function-calling boundary fix
tail.summary: Ollama added first-class Nemotron 3 architecture support and shipped `ollama run nemotron-3.5-lightning` on the same day as NVIDIA's launch, alongside a fix for a boundary condition in Muse Glimmer function calling. NVIDIA's framing in the release notes is telling — the model is aimed at harnesses like OpenClaw and Hermes Agent under NVIDIA's own NemoClaw security and management stack, i.e. always-on agents rather than chat. The function-calling boundary fix is worth noting if you tested Muse Glimmer tool use in the first 48 hours and found it flaky; that was partly the runtime.

tail.title: First community GGUF of Ling-3.0-tiny lands, and it is the one open release this week that comfortably fits 16GB
tail.summary: A day after inclusionAI published the MIT-licensed Ling-3.0-tiny weights, the first community GGUF ladder appeared, and the sizes are the opposite story to Nemotron: Q4_K_M 4.82GB, MXFP4_MOE 4.72GB, Q5_K_M 5.64GB, Q6_K 6.50GB, Q8_0 8.41GB, BF16 15.80GB. Q8_0 fits a 5060 Ti with more than 7GB spare for context, which means you can run this at near-lossless precision rather than paying the multiplicative quantisation penalty at all. For any experiment where you need a small open model whose quantisation is not a confound, this is currently the best-positioned option on your card.

tail.title: ggml-org publishes a one-command Nemotron 3.5 Lightning GGUF — the smallest of which is 22.46GB
tail.summary: The official ggml-org repo carries a 264-character card whose entire content is `llama-server -hf ggml-org/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-GGUF`, and four files: NVFP4 22.46GB, Q4_K_M 25.43GB, Q8_0 35.00GB, BF16 65.85GB. The one-command story is genuinely good ergonomics and completely irrelevant if you have 16GB, since the smallest artefact is 40% larger than your card. The BF16 figure also pins the true parameter count at roughly 33B, not the 30B in the marketing name.

tail.title: A '5GB' Nemotron 3.5 Lightning repo is a 25.4GB Q4_K_M cut into six pieces
tail.summary: The repo name reads as a 5GB model and the card is honest about what it actually is: a Q4_K_M quant run through llama-gguf-split with --split-max-size 5G, producing six shards of 4.60/4.42/4.62/4.85/4.65/2.30GB for 25.44GB total. Nothing is misrepresented in the card, but the repo name alone is exactly the sort of thing that gets cited as evidence a 30B runs in 5GB. It is also a useful independent confirmation of bartowski's 24.73GB Q4_K_M figure, from a different quantiser.

tail.title: MODEL-CLAIM RESOLVED: strawberry-1 now declares a base model — and its quant ladder is flat from Q2 to IQ4
tail.summary: The carry-forward flag on mradermacher/strawberry-1-GGUF is closed: the card now carries base_model artindnr/strawberry-1, a Persian/English MXFP4 mixture-of-experts model, so the provenance gap is answered. A new observation replaces it — the published quant sizes are Q2_K 12.2GB, Q3_K_S 12.2GB and IQ4_XS 12.3GB, a 0.1GB spread across a 2-bit-to-4-bit range, the same flat-ladder signature seen today on Nemotron. Two independent MXFP4/hybrid MoE releases showing it in one window suggests a systematic llama.cpp quantisation behaviour on these architectures rather than two coincidental bad uploads.

tail.title: MODEL-CLAIM STILL OPEN: the Kimi K3 2-bit KLD-0.08 repo has sat at two files for two days
tail.summary: lukealonso/Kimi-K3-QSRT-K2 still contains exactly two files, a 339-character README reading 'upload in progress... slowly' and no config.json, while advertising a 2-bit quant of Kimi K3 at a KLD of 0.08 with 'surprisingly strong coding/benchmark performance' on 8x RTX 6000 or 6-8 DGX Spark. The only substantive artefact is the QSRT 2bpw codec document in the local-inference-lab repo, which is at least a real technical description. Verdict unchanged from yesterday: the claim is unevaluable because the weights it describes do not exist yet, and a KLD figure with no reference distribution or calibration corpus named is not a number anyone can reproduce.

tail.title: HYGIENE CLOSED: both VideoGuard safety models are now ungated, with full cards and configs
tail.summary: The flag raised yesterday — safety-evaluation models published gated while ungated GGUF quants of the same weights circulated — has resolved in the right direction. Both the 4B and 9B VideoGuard repos now return gated:false with README (14,974 and 12,632 characters) and config.json serving on the open API, nine files each. The evaluation surface is now inspectable, which is the condition for taking a safety-classifier claim seriously at all. Adoption is nil so far: one like and zero recorded downloads on each.

tail.title: CARRY-FORWARD HYGIENE: Tess-4.1 401s for a sixth run, AMD's Whisper NPU repo is down to two files, VibeWorlder still has no card
tail.summary: Three carry-forward flags remain open with no movement. migtissera/Tess-4.1-35B-A3B returns 401 on API, README and config for the sixth consecutive check, which at this point should be read as permanently withdrawn rather than transiently broken, and community imatrix quants of it are still being published against a base nobody can fetch. amd/whisper-large-v3-turbo-onnx-npu resolves on the API but still 404s README and config and now lists just two files. usail-hkust/VibeWorlder-8B serves a config and 21 files but has never published a card, six days after upload, with four recorded downloads.

tail.title: llama.cpp b10355 lands multi-output backend sampling, letting speculation sample on-device
tail.summary: PR #25532 enables backend sampling with token speculation, adding a numeric context parameter that declares the maximum number of outputs and clamping the mask sum before it becomes a sampled index. Keeping sampling on the accelerator during speculative decoding removes a per-step host round-trip, which is where a good share of the latency in draft-and-verify setups actually goes. A follow-up build the next day had to disable the new multi-output test on HIP because top_k's backend probability path needs CUB, so AMD users should expect this to be CUDA-first.

tail.title: NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard routes agent workloads across models instead of picking one
tail.summary: Published the same day as Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and clearly designed to sell it, Switchyard is NVIDIA's routing layer for sending each step of an agent task to a different model — classification here, reasoning there, a small model for follow-up. The strategic read matters more than the product: NVIDIA is positioning Lightning as the cheap execution tier that a frontier planner delegates to, which is the same architecture OpenRouter's Auto router and Sakana's Fugu conductor are converging on from different directions. Routing decisions are themselves a judge problem, and none of these three publish how the router is evaluated.

tail.title: Ollama v0.32.8 brings Muse Glimmer to every platform after two days of Apple-Silicon-only support
tail.summary: v0.32.7 shipped Muse Glimmer through the MLX engine on Apple Silicon only, with NVIDIA and AMD promised 'in the coming days'; v0.32.8 delivered them a day later, so `ollama run muse-glimmer` now works on a CUDA card. The release also points at driving Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw and Hermes from the local model. Given the 16GB numbers, on your card this routes to a Q3-class quant in practice, not the default tag Ollama will pull.

tail.title: Red Hat AI publishes an NVFP4 Muse Glimmer built with llm-compressor for vLLM
tail.summary: Red Hat's compressed-tensors NVFP4 build of Muse Glimmer is 23.41GB across two shards, produced with the llm-compressor 0.13.0 model-free PTQ recipe and targeted at vLLM rather than llama.cpp. NVFP4 needs Blackwell-class FP4 tensor cores to pay off, which your 5060 Ti has, but at 23.41GB the weights do not fit regardless of format support. It is the reference artefact for how the FP4 path is being productionised, and useful as a size comparison against the 4-bit GGUF and EXL3 rungs.

tail.title: most-embed-de: a 2.28GB German retrieval embedder built on Ministral3
tail.summary: A sentence-transformers retrieval model for German built on the Ministral3 backbone, shipped as a single 2.28GB safetensors file with MTEB claims in a 9,255-character card. At that size it runs alongside a generation model on a 16GB card without contention, which is the practical criterion for an embedder in a local RAG stack. MTEB numbers on a language-specific model are worth checking against the specific German subsets rather than the headline average, since the aggregate is dominated by tasks a multilingual baseline already handles.

tail.title: Fastino publishes domain-specialised Nemotron 3.5 Lightning fine-tunes for finance and healthcare
tail.summary: Fastino has finance and healthcare verticalisations of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, uploaded 6 August — before the model's public launch, which confirms partner pre-access. A healthcare-domain fine-tune of a model whose own bias card reports a BBQ metric with no score is precisely the configuration where demographic-bias auditing has teeth, since the clinical application is where the downstream harm lands and the base disclosure gives you nothing to compare against.

tail.title: IBM Research argues ACE-style agentic context engineering can be done with far fewer tokens
tail.summary: IBM Research's ALTK post takes aim at the token cost of ACE-style agentic context engineering, proposing an evolve/SLDD approach that claims comparable results at materially lower token spend. Token-efficiency claims in this genre are usually reported against the authors' own baseline configuration rather than a tuned one, so the number to look for is whether they held the task and harness fixed. Relevant if you are costing multi-turn judge pipelines where context assembly, not generation, dominates the bill.

tail.title: Sakana retrains its Fugu conductor on Gemma 4 to show orchestration does not depend on the base model
tail.summary: Sakana trained the conductor model of its Fugu orchestration system on a Gemma 4 base and reports orchestration performance equivalent to the previous version, framing the result as base-model-independence in service of sovereignty requirements — a customer who cannot use a given base can still get the orchestration layer. The claim is a negative one (swapping the base did not degrade performance), which is the harder kind to trust without the evaluation detail; the post is in Japanese and does not surface a benchmark table in the summary. Structurally interesting as a modular alternative to routing: diversify the conductor, not just the pool.

tail.title: Mistral commits to in-region inference and new European infrastructure for sovereign AI
tail.summary: Mistral bundled in-region inference guarantees, continued open-model releases and new European compute commitments into a single sovereignty roadmap. The open-models element is the part with technical consequence — a vendor tying open weights to a sovereignty argument has a structural reason to keep releasing them, which is a different incentive from the ones driving Meta's and NVIDIA's open releases. Data-residency guarantees also matter directly if any consulting work involves EU client data passing through a model API.

tail.title: Lightricks ships an LTX-2.5 spatial upscaler IC-LoRA — and auto-gates it
tail.summary: An in-context LoRA for LTX-2.5 22B doing video-to-video spatial upscaling and super-resolution, three files, four likes on its first day. It carries gated:auto, so the API returns metadata but README and config both 401 without accepting terms — meaning the technical claims cannot be checked from outside the gate. That is the same gated-eval-surface pattern flagged on VideoGuard yesterday, resolved there today and appearing here instead.

tail.title: llama.cpp moves its release builds to ROCm 7.14, the first production TheRock build
tail.summary: CI switched from ROCm 7.2.1 to 7.14, described in the commit as the first production release using the TheRock build system, installable from multi-arch wheels, debs and rpms. Irrelevant to a CUDA card directly, but it is the upstream change that will determine whether AMD users get comparable kernel coverage over the next few months — and today's HIP test disablement on the new multi-output sampler shows how far behind that path still is.

tail.title: llama.cpp b10361 fixes sliding-window attention silently never enabling for EXAONE 4.5
tail.summary: load_arch_hparams tested hparams.n_layer() == 64 before LLM_KV_NEXTN_PREDICT_LAYERS had been read, so SWA never turned on for EXAONE 4.5 — a silent correctness-and-memory bug rather than a crash. This is the second ordering bug of its kind in llama.cpp's loader in a week (b10338 fixed a GGUF round-trip that broke shared-expert MoEs on reload). If you benchmarked EXAONE 4.5 locally before this build, the KV-cache footprint and long-context behaviour you measured were not the intended ones.

tail.title: Muse Glimmer AWQ-INT4 arrives at 24.04GB as the community hunts for a 16GB-viable cut
tail.summary: An AWQ INT4 build across five shards totalling 24.04GB — nominally 4-bit yet larger than the 16.94GB Q4_K_M GGUF of the same model, because AWQ leaves more of the network in higher precision and does not apply GGUF's per-block scheme to every tensor. A useful reminder that 'INT4' names a method, not a footprint, and that comparing quantisation methods by bit label rather than measured bytes will mislead you. It does not fit a 5060 Ti.

tail.title: Claude Code v2.1.228 fixes /tui silently reverting the session to an older model
tail.summary: The fix list includes /tui reverting a session to an earlier model when /model had been changed since the last response, interactive sessions that stopped redrawing entirely while the process kept running, and git not being found on Windows when Claude Code is launched from a parent folder of the git installation. The model-reversion bug is the one with research consequences: a session that silently downgrades mid-task produces output attributed to a model that did not generate it. The Windows git path fix is directly relevant to this machine.

tail.title: Claude Code v2.1.227 fixes Max-plan users being wrongly prompted to buy usage credits
tail.summary: Feature flags were being evaluated without the user's subscription tier when a session started with an expired login token, which could wrongly prompt Max plan users to enable paid usage credits for Fable. Also fixed: every Bash command failing under claude-code-action with allowed_non_write_users on GitHub-hosted runners, and /tui restoring a conversation that had been rewound past its first message. Worth knowing if you saw an unexpected credit prompt in the last week — it was a bug, not your plan.

tail.title: FastMCP v3.4.7 fixes a doubled-slash audience mismatch breaking private_key_jwt auth
tail.summary: The patch restores CIMD private_key_jwt authentication for OAuthProxy deployments served at a bare origin, by validating client assertions against the exact token endpoint advertised in authorization server metadata instead of a URL with a doubled slash. This is the third consecutive FastMCP release in a week dealing with proxy and OAuth correctness, following the SSRF-safe proxy work in 3.4.6. If you run any MCP server behind an auth proxy, this is the branch to be on rather than 4.0.0b2.

tail.title: LiteLLM v1.96.0 documents cosign verification against a commit-pinned public key
tail.summary: Every LiteLLM Docker image is now signed with cosign, and the release notes give the verification command against a raw GitHub URL pinned to a specific commit hash rather than a branch — the point being that a commit hash is immutable, so fetching the key that way cannot be swapped under you. This is a small but genuinely correct supply-chain practice worth copying if you ever publish a container for an eval harness.

tail.title: Langfuse ships v4.7.0 through v4.9.0 in a single day
tail.summary: Four Langfuse releases inside twelve hours (4.7.0, 4.7.1, 4.8.0, 4.9.0) plus a 3.x backport at 3.225.2, following 4.5.0 and 4.6.0 the day before. That cadence on an observability backend that stores your trace history is a pinning question rather than an upgrade question: if a judge run's traces need to be readable in six months, pin the version and the schema. The 3.x backport indicates the v3 line is still supported for anyone who has not migrated.

tail.title: Arize Phoenix client v3.0.0 breaks the Gemini formatter and moves PXI tracing server-side
tail.summary: The breaking change is replacing the google-generativeai formatter with google-genai, matching Google's own SDK deprecation. Also landing: REST CRUD for user and system API keys, REST endpoints for experiment tags, dataset example source-span exposure, and agent tracing moved server-side. The dataset and experiment REST surface is the part that makes a scripted eval pipeline reproducible without clicking through a UI.

tail.title: ExLlamaV3 1.4.2 ships with no release notes at all
tail.summary: The tag carries an entirely empty body, which in isolation looks like nothing — but turboderp's Muse Glimmer EXL3 quants published the same evening state they require exactly v1.4.2 or the dev branch, so the release is the Muse Glimmer architecture support. This follows v1.4.0 adding DeepSeek V4 and v1.4.1 adding Mistral-4 in the preceding three days. Empty release bodies on this repo should be read as 'see the quant repo published alongside it', not as a fetch failure.

tail.title: Jiunsong publishes a 116-file abliterated DeepSeek-V4-Flash sized for two DGX boxes
tail.summary: An FP4 mixed-quant abliterated DeepSeek-V4-Flash across 116 files with a 9,961-character card, explicitly sized to a two-DGX target rather than a consumer card. The naming convention encoding the hardware target into the repo name is a small good practice — it tells you the deployment envelope before you start a download. Nothing here is runnable locally; it is a data point on how far the refusal-ablation wave has climbed up the parameter scale in a week.

tail.title: dealignai ships an NVFP4 'CRACK' DeepSeek-V4-Flash aimed straight at vLLM
tail.summary: An abliterated DeepSeek-V4-Flash in NVFP4 across 77 files, tagged for vLLM serving, from the same account that published a CRACK GGUF of Muse Glimmer the same day. 'CRACK' is a third naming convention for suppression removal alongside abliterated and heretic, and none of the three are defined anywhere shared — which is itself a problem for anyone trying to compare methods, since the label tells you nothing about whether it was a directional ablation, a fine-tune, or a merge.

tail.title: A ternary-class TQ3_4S quant of DeepSeek-V4-Flash lands with an explicit recipe
tail.summary: A 13-file GGUF using the TQ3_4S ternary-family quantisation on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, with a 4,459-character card documenting the recipe. Extreme-low-bit quants of large MoEs are where the multiplicative damage argument bites hardest — at 3 bits the retained margin is around a third, and below that it collapses — so a card that publishes its recipe is at least auditable, which most in this class are not. Eight likes on day one.

tail.title: NVIDIA's own NVFP4 Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is roughly 19GB across 52 shards
tail.summary: The first-party NVFP4 release sums to about 19GB over 52 safetensors shards with a highly irregular shard pattern — alternating 0.73GB and 0.04GB files with a single 3.60GB tail — which is consistent with the hybrid architecture keeping some layer types out of the 4-bit path. It is the smallest first-party artefact NVIDIA publishes and it is still 3GB above a 16GB card. Three independent quantisers now agree the model has no 16GB-viable form.

tail.title: MiniMax-H3 hybrid merges appear, stitching first-and-last-frame and reference-to-video models together
tail.summary: A merge of the FL2VA and REF2VA MiniMax-H3 variants into hybrid checkpoints supporting text-to-video, image-to-video and synchronised audio-video from one model, twelve likes in a day. Merging two task-specialised diffusion transformers rather than switching between them is an efficiency move for a constrained VRAM budget, but merged diffusion models routinely lose fidelity on both parent tasks and no comparison against either parent is published here.

tail.title: A quantized MiniMax-H3 Turbo GGUF fits the DiT in 16GB but not the full pipeline
tail.summary: The FL2VA pruned DiT with the LightX2V 8-step turbo LoRA baked in, published as a split ComfyUI-ready set: DiT at Q3_K_M 8.72GB, Q4_K_M 11.39GB, Q6_K 16.56GB, Q8_0 21.42GB, plus a 5.24GB Qwen3-VL 4B text encoder, a 5.21GB video VAE and a 0.61GB audio VAE. On a 16GB card the Q3 or Q4 DiT fits but the full stack does not — you need ComfyUI sequential offload to move the text encoder and VAEs on and off, which works but costs wall-clock per frame. Sample videos are included, which is more than most video quant repos provide.

tail.title: Motif-3 finally gets a community GGUF — a single Q5_K_M split across 228GB
tail.summary: The first community GGUF of Motif-3 offers exactly one rung, Q5_K_M, across five shards totalling 228.54GB, behind a 390-character card. A single high-precision quant of a model this size serves nobody without a cluster, and there is no imatrix, no smaller rung and no evaluation. It is a placeholder for a quant ladder rather than a usable one.

tail.title: A 'derisked' Ling-3.0-flash GGUF ships as two files and no config
tail.summary: Tagged abliterated and uncensored under the euphemism 'derisked', this repo has two files, no config.json and a 4,110-character card. 'Derisked' joins abliterated, heretic and CRACK as a fourth undefined term for suppression removal in a single collection window. The proliferation of labels without shared definitions is a genuine obstacle to studying the phenomenon: you cannot compare methods when the method name is chosen for vibe rather than technique.

tail.title: An 'OBLITERATED' DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B shows the abliteration wave reaching 1.5B models
tail.summary: Refusal ablation applied to a 1.5B distilled reasoning model, shipped as both safetensors and GGUF with 'obliteratus' among its tags. At 1.5B the whole model fits in VRAM many times over, which makes this size class the practical one for running an ablation study with many conditions rather than one heroic run. Whether refusal directions in a distilled 1.5B behave like those in a 30B is an open empirical question and cheap to test on your hardware.

tail.title: NVIDIA JetPack 7.2.1 adds agentic video skills and T3000 emulation to Jetson
tail.summary: JetPack 7.2.1 packages the camera-capture, decode, inference, annotate and encode chain into composable 'agentic video skills' and adds emulation of the T3000 part so developers can target unreleased hardware. Edge-side, this is the same architectural bet as Nemotron Lightning: small always-on models doing high-volume execution rather than a single large call. Third-tier relevance unless a consulting engagement touches embedded deployment.

tail.title: Unsloth v0.1.62-beta ships as 'many bug fixes' hours before the Desktop launch
tail.summary: A release body reading in full 'Many bug fixes', tagged three hours before Unsloth Desktop. Unsloth has now cut releases under two parallel version schemes in three days — v0.1.60 through v0.1.62 alongside v0.1.525 through v0.1.527 and then v0.1.70/v0.1.701 — which makes 'what version am I on' genuinely ambiguous. If you pin Unsloth for a fine-tuning run, pin the commit.

tail.title: stable-diffusion.cpp cuts two master builds in one evening
tail.summary: Builds 815 and 816 landed roughly an hour apart with no release notes, continuing the rolling-master release pattern this project uses instead of semantic versions. For a local image stack this means the only way to know what changed is the commit log; there is no changelog to read. Relevant only if you run the C++ diffusion path rather than ComfyUI.

tail.title: OpenAI begins testing advertisements inside ChatGPT
tail.summary: OpenAI announced ad testing in ChatGPT, promising clear labelling, answer independence from advertiser influence, privacy protections and user control. 'Answer independence' is the load-bearing claim and the only one that is empirically testable from outside: whether responses shift toward advertised products in the presence of an ad slot is a measurable behavioural question, and nobody has published a protocol for it. This is the sort of claim that becomes an auditable research question the moment the feature ships broadly.

tail.title: Google ships gemini-cli v0.56.0-preview.1 amid a nightly cadence
tail.summary: gemini-cli cut a v0.56.0 preview alongside v0.55.0-preview.3 and two dated nightlies in the same 48-hour window. Four release channels running concurrently (stable, preview, nightly, and dated nightly builds) means a bare version number does not identify a build. Worth a glance if you use gemini-cli as a delegation target for read-heavy work.

tail.title: Qwen Live Host v0.1.1 appears alongside qwen-code v0.21.10
tail.summary: A separately versioned 'Live Host' component now ships out of the qwen-code repository at v0.1.1, distinct from the CLI's own v0.21.10, suggesting a hosted or long-running session surface is being split out of the CLI. Early enough that no documentation accompanies the tag. Note the standing warning that qwen.ai/blog and qwenlm.github.io are both dead or frozen, so the repository is the only reliable Qwen source.

tail.title: OpenAI's Python SDK reaches v2.54.0
tail.summary: A routine minor release of the official Python SDK, cut the same day as openai-agents-python v0.20.0 changed its implicit default model. If you pin one of these two, pin both — the agents library's behaviour depends on the SDK version underneath it, and the default-model change means an unpinned pair can shift which model answered a request between two runs of the same script.

tail.title: Cline ships a full SDK matrix at v0.0.73 plus CLI v3.0.53
tail.summary: Cline tagged five SDK packages (core, shared, llms, agents, and the umbrella sdk) at v0.0.73 within the same minute, alongside CLI v3.0.53 and the extension at v4.1.8. The move to a published, separately versioned SDK matrix suggests Cline is positioning as an embeddable agent runtime rather than only a VS Code extension — the same direction Claude Code took with its agent SDK. Still v0.0.x, so treat the interface as unstable.

tail.title: Mem0 cuts Python and Node SDK releases within a minute of each other
tail.summary: Mem0 released Python SDK v2.0.18 and Node SDK v3.1.6 sixty seconds apart, keeping the two language bindings in lockstep despite divergent major versions. Memory layers for agents are an area worth tracking given your own LKHS setup; the question to ask of any of them is what retrieval guarantees they make, since 'memory' in this product category usually means embedding search with no recall guarantee at all.

tail.title: 100 errors planted in 10 psychology papers: best AI reviewer caught 71, pooling every system caught 93
tail.summary: Paul Litvak inserted 100 known errors into 10 open-access psychology papers and ran them past frontier models plus two commercial AI review tools; the best single system found 71, the worst 30, and the union found 93. Overlap between systems was low, the 7 nobody caught were all omissions rather than inserted mistakes, and false positives were not measured at all. Papers, errors, model outputs and full logs are on GitHub — this is a ready-made ensemble-vs-single-judge dataset in your exact domain, and the missing false-positive arm is the obvious contribution you could add.

tail.title: LTX-2.5: an open-weights video world model tuned for consumer RTX cards, native in ComfyUI
tail.summary: Lightricks released LTX-2.5 as open weights on HuggingFace, free for organisations under $10M revenue, with NVIDIA-side optimisation aimed explicitly at cutting VRAM so it runs on hardware people already own, and native ComfyUI availability. This is a different family from the MiniMax-H3 nodes that have flooded your feed for a fortnight, so it is a genuine second option rather than another H3 accelerator; worth a slot in the ComfyUI/WAN stack specifically because the tuning target is the consumer card rather than a GB200.

tail.title: Kokoro-FastAPI v0.8.0-rc1
tail.summary: A release candidate for the OpenAI-compatible serving layer around the Kokoro TTS model. This is the engine underneath your audio-overview and long-form-audio skills, so a version bump here is the difference between a working narration pipeline and a broken one — worth reading the changelog before it becomes the default and worth pinning if your local setup is stable.

tail.title: Handy: fully offline push-to-talk dictation with Whisper or Parakeet V3, Windows NVIDIA supported
tail.summary: Press a shortcut, speak, and transcribed text lands in whatever field has focus — no audio leaves the machine. Whisper Small through Large with GPU acceleration, plus Parakeet V3 which runs CPU-only at ~5x realtime with automatic language detection, on Windows with NVIDIA support. Rust backend, React frontend, and the project deliberately advertises itself as the most forkable STT app. For drafting fiction or dictating notes into Obsidian this is a lower-friction input path than typing, and it stays inside your no-cloud constraint.

tail.title: Forma: a local-first reading workspace where you select an equation and your own Claude Code CLI explains it
tail.summary: The PDF stays in the browser; only the extracted text and your selection go to a locally signed-in agent (Claude Code CLI, Codex app-server, or Gemini CLI), and conversations are ephemeral and stored only in Forma rather than in cloud history. It explicitly separates paper-grounded claims from outside background knowledge. That separation is the useful part for you — it is the same distinction your paper-claim-audit workflow enforces, applied at read time instead of at write time, on your existing subscriptions rather than API credits.

tail.title: Stratawright: an agentic DAW your coding agent drives in plain English
tail.summary: A C++20 audio engine plus a daw-cli skill that lets Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Gemini do real production work — set tempo, import stems, place clips, auto-colour tracks by instrument, insert VST3/AU plugins, copy mixing chains, sequence MIDI drums, detect frequency masking and watch LUFS. CC BY 4.0, builds with CMake and vcpkg. It is the first agent-controlled music tool that does mixing rather than generation, which makes it interesting for scoring or sound design where you want your own audio, not a model's.

tail.title: Scroll through all 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 states of a Rubik's Cube
tail.summary: An infinite-scroll page that indexes the full cube state space and renders whichever position corresponds to your scroll offset, which means the page is really a bijection between a scrollbar and a 4.3x10^19-element group. Nothing to install and nothing to do with AI — it is here because it is the cleanest demonstration this week of making an incomprehensible number physically scrollable, which is a presentation trick worth stealing for any figure about scale.

tail.title: antirez wrote a from-scratch MiniMax-H3 inference engine in C for Apple Silicon
tail.summary: The Redis author's h3.c is a native Metal implementation of MiniMax-H3 inference with no framework underneath it, in the same tradition as his earlier from-scratch model code. The hardware target is wrong for your 5060 Ti, but the codebase is the point: a readable single-purpose engine is the fastest way to actually understand how an omni-modal model's decode loop is wired, versus reading around vLLM.

tail.title: Text AI watermarks will always be trivial to remove
tail.summary: Published the same week Anthropic committed to embedding watermarks in Claude-generated text, this argues the text case is structurally different from images: paraphrase destroys the signal and the cost of paraphrasing is one more model call. Directly relevant to the AI-footprint scrubber in your mimesis pipeline — if the argument holds, a scrubber that already rewrites for style is incidentally a watermark stripper, which is a provenance question you may want an answer to before someone asks.

tail.title: Stories of people finding weird, wild and defiant ways to avoid using AI at work
tail.summary: A collection of accounts from people quietly refusing AI mandates — including someone keeping a paper to-do list while their boss believes they run a Claude task assistant. It is the culture-side mirror of the adoption stories, and useful raw material if you ever write about organisational AI mandates for the leadership-report work, because it is refusal as workplace behaviour rather than as opinion.

tail.title: Temperature Zero for Culture: why everything is starting to look the same
tail.summary: An argument that widespread generative tooling collapses cultural variance the way a temperature-0 decode collapses token variance — the mode wins everywhere. It gives you a precise, sampling-theoretic vocabulary for the thing your voice-cloning work is fighting: a stylometric fingerprint is only defensible if the ambient distribution has not already flattened toward the mode.

tail.title: How I used an LLM to kick my nicotine addiction
tail.summary: No tool and no app — one long-running chat thread the author returned to at every craving, which re-served a framework they had already internalised from two books, at midnight, without getting tired of repeating itself. The author is unusually honest that the LLM contributed no original insight and would have failed without the prior reframing. That is a clean n-of-1 description of the just-in-time adaptive intervention mechanism your Baseline app is built around: the model as retrieval-and-delivery for a framework the user already holds.

tail.title: I made tinnitus my friend, then it disappeared
tail.summary: The creator of myNoise describes reframing tinnitus from threat to neutral background and reports habituation following. It is a first-person account of an attentional-reappraisal mechanism with a soundscape tool attached, which is the same class of intervention your anhedonia tracker is instrumenting — and a reminder that the measurable thing is often attention allocation rather than the symptom.

tail.title: Spotify will badge 'AI Persona' artists and drop them out of recommendations
tail.summary: From mid-September, artist profiles that do not represent a real person get an AI Persona badge and are excluded by default from editorial, algorithmic and personalised recommendations. This is a platform choosing suppression over labelling-only, which is a much stronger provenance regime than the watermarking commitments announced the same week — and a live test case of what happens to reach when disclosure is enforced.

tail.title: D'Addario admits Suno Studio was used to 'regenerate the track' in a string demo, then disavows AI music
tail.summary: A guitar-string manufacturer got caught using generative audio in a demo whose whole point was how the strings sound, apologised, and committed to a disclosure process. The specific comedy — AI-generating the demonstration of a physical product's timbre — is the sharpest example this week of where audiences actually draw the line, which is not 'AI was used' but 'AI was used in the thing being demonstrated'.

tail.title: The Carcass: a cosmic roguelike whose AI disclosure was on the demo page but not the full game page
tail.summary: RPS covered a genuinely striking premise — colony-building inside a slowly-waking god — then updated the piece after finding an AI disclosure on the demo's separate Steam page while the main page carried none. A small, concrete illustration of how disclosure regimes fail in practice: the requirement existed, was met once, and was invisible where it mattered.

tail.title: How a debut self-published novel earned five figures in ten weeks without Kindle Unlimited
tail.summary: A marketing consultant of 25 years applied her own client question — what is your goal — to a six-month pre-launch plan for her first novel, with no platform and no publisher, and refused the Kindle Unlimited exclusivity trade. It is a concrete costed alternative to the two default paths for The Basilisk, and the pre-launch structure is the part that transfers regardless of genre.

tail.title: John Crowley (1942-2026)
tail.summary: Locus's obituary for the author of Little, Big and the Aegypt sequence, who died 8 August at 83. Crowley is one of the small set of writers who made literary-register fantasy respectable in the genre, and the obituary doubles as a reading map if you have only encountered him by reputation.

tail.title: Tea Obreht on writing a layered, intertextual tale of the American West
tail.summary: A craft interview about building a novel that treats the Western as genre, as theatre and as propaganda simultaneously, from the author of The Tiger's Wife. The useful part is her account of layering registers inside one book without the seams showing, which is the structural problem in any novel that runs myth and realism in the same paragraph.

tail.title: Agentic World Cup: LLMs playing 1v1 soccer against each other
tail.summary: A live arena where different models control players in continuous 1v1 matches, with results accumulating into a leaderboard. It is a toy, but it is also a head-to-head eval with a non-language action space and an unambiguous outcome variable — the kind of arena where the usual judge biases cannot operate, which makes it a useful contrast case when you are arguing about what LLM-as-judge can and cannot substitute for.

tail.title: A 60-second cognitive test that tries to tell humans from bots without a camera
tail.summary: A browser challenge that profiles response-time distributions and error patterns rather than asking you to identify traffic lights, on the theory that human cognition leaves a timing signature a model does not reproduce. Whether or not it survives contact with a determined attacker, it is a psychometrics-flavoured take on bot detection, and the underlying construct — reaction-time variability as an identity signal — is testable with the same tooling you use for judge calibration.

tail.title: wikicompare: read the same Wikipedia article across languages, side by side
tail.summary: A tool for diffing the same topic across language editions, launched with Middle East articles as the demo case, which surfaces the framing and omission differences that a monolingual reader never sees. This is a cheap source of natural language-pair bias data — the multilingual version of the demographic-swap design in PsychBench, with human editors rather than a model producing the variants.

tail.title: mcp-tester: profile any MCP server for latency, token usage and security holes
tail.summary: Points at an MCP server and reports per-tool latency, the token cost of its tool definitions, and a security scan of what it exposes. The token-cost number is the one that matters for you — every MCP server you leave connected eats context in every session, and this measures the tax before you decide which of your dozen-plus servers stay loaded.

tail.title: Blender MCP maintainer's GitHub account was hacked
tail.summary: The maintainer of one of the more widely installed MCP servers reported their account compromised. MCP servers run with your credentials and file access by design, so a compromised upstream is a compromised machine — this is the concrete reason to actually run something like mcp-tester over the servers you have installed and to pin versions rather than tracking main.

tail.title: gsheets-mcp: a small self-hosted MCP giving Claude read/write on your Google Sheets
tail.summary: A minimal server rather than a platform integration, which is the version you want when the alternative is granting a hosted service access to your Drive. Useful if any part of your eval bookkeeping or deadline tracking lives in a sheet — it turns 'read the scores tab and tell me the effective N' into a single tool call instead of an export.

tail.title: Etincel: train Claude to write PR reviews and code comments in a specific voice
tail.summary: A skill that conditions Claude's review-comment register on examples rather than on adjectives — same core move as your mimesis corpus anchoring, applied to a much narrower and more measurable output type. Worth reading for how it handles the small-corpus case, because PR comments give you far fewer tokens to fingerprint against than a novel does.

tail.title: context-mode: sandbox agent tool output and cut it 98%
tail.summary: Intercepts tool results before they hit the context window, stores the full output out of band, and passes a compact handle plus summary instead, with session memory persisted across runs. The claimed reduction is 98%. This is the exact failure mode of a collector run — a 22MB arXiv harvest dumped into context — and the pattern is worth stealing even if you do not adopt the tool.

tail.title: mcptoon: a token-efficient MCP CLI client
tail.summary: A command-line MCP client built around minimising the token footprint of tool schemas and responses. Handy for the debugging case you actually hit — checking whether an MCP server is alive and what it returns — without spinning up a full agent session just to call one tool.

tail.title: Orca: run a fleet of parallel coding agents on your own subscription
tail.summary: An agentic development environment for orchestrating many coding agents at once, deliberately built to run against your existing subscription rather than metered API keys. If you ever want to fan a task across parallel agents the way your master-context skill does, this is the general-purpose version — and the subscription-not-API design is the part that keeps a wide fan-out from becoming a bill.

tail.title: OpenMontage: an open-source agentic video production system with 700+ agent skills
tail.summary: Twelve production pipelines, 100+ tools and a very large skill library aimed at end-to-end video assembly rather than clip generation. The interesting claim is the split — generation models make shots, this makes a cut — which is the missing half of every local video-gen stack including the ComfyUI one. Worth a look if a research explainer or conference talk ever needs video rather than slides.

tail.title: claude-obsidian: a self-organising second brain where Claude files and links your notes
tail.summary: Drop a source into a folder and Claude Code reads it, links it against existing notes and files it in your Obsidian vault. This is adjacent to what LKHS already does for conversation memory, but it operates on documents you drop in rather than sessions you have — potentially the ingestion path for papers and clippings that currently never make it into any index.

tail.title: microsandbox: a local-first microVM runtime for giving agents somewhere safe to run
tail.summary: Fast local microVMs as a library, positioned for exactly the case where you want an agent to execute arbitrary code without it being your machine. This is the self-hosted counterpart to the hosted sandbox products, and the relevant question for you is whether it makes --dangerously-skip-permissions a defensible setting on a Windows box rather than a gamble.

tail.title: Easy sandboxing on Linux with Bubblewrap
tail.summary: A practical walkthrough of bwrap for confining a process's filesystem and network view without containers or root. The lightest-weight option in the agent-sandboxing space this week, and the one that works today inside WSL if you want to fence a scraping or eval script off from the rest of the machine.

tail.title: Making etched holograms with a pen plotter
tail.summary: Scratch holograms made by having a pen plotter draw precise arcs on acrylic, so the specular highlights track your eye and a 3D image resolves out of pure geometry. No optics, no lasers, no computation — just the right arcs. A very satisfying demonstration that a plotter is a general-purpose precision instrument rather than a drawing toy.

tail.title: LUMEN-PS: turn a flatbed scanner into a photometric-stereo material scanner
tail.summary: Exploits the fact that a flatbed's moving light bar illuminates the subject from a known changing angle, so several passes give you the varying-illumination stack photometric stereo needs to recover surface normals. It turns a $60 scanner into a normal-map capture rig for texturing. Cheapest route to real material scans if anything in the ComfyUI or 3D side of your stack ever wants them.

tail.title: Mastering edge AI on Raspberry Pi with LiteRT and Gemma
tail.summary: Google's LiteRT runtime has had substantial performance work done specifically for Raspberry Pi, with Gemma as the worked example. Relevant if you want an always-on inference node that is not your workstation — a Pi running a small model is enough to host a local classifier or an always-listening transcription endpoint without keeping the 5060 Ti awake.

tail.title: A Three.js simulator for today's total solar eclipse
tail.summary: A browser simulator for the 12 August 2026 totality path, letting you pick a location and watch the geometry play out. Timely to the day. Not AI at all — it is here because a well-built physical simulation is a better explanation of an eclipse than any amount of prose, and because it is happening now.

tail.title: There's a dungeon under this blog
tail.summary: A personal site with a playable dungeon crawler hidden beneath the post list, written up as a build log. Pure delight, and a good reminder that a personal site can be an artefact rather than a CV — worth thinking about if the publication-pipeline work ever gets a public front page.

tail.title: The Odyssey was for sailors: a D3 visual essay
tail.summary: An argument about the Odyssey's intended audience made through interactive maps and charts of its geography and sailing detail rather than through prose alone. It is the format your own explanatory writing keeps reaching for — claim, then a figure that makes the claim inspectable — executed well enough to steal the structure from.

tail.title: Memo Dungeon: a browser roguelike where you fight by memorising strings
tail.summary: Combat is recall — you are shown a string, it disappears, and you type it back under pressure, with difficulty scaling by length and character set. It is a working-memory span task wearing a roguelike costume, which makes it a surprisingly clean piece of gamified psychometrics and a nice example of how to make a boring measure voluntarily repeated.

tail.title: sqnc.run: a live cipher stream in the style of a numbers station
tail.summary: A continuously broadcasting page of encoded sequences with no explanation, deliberately reproducing the affect of shortwave numbers stations. Strange, atmospheric, and useful as ambience or as a prompt object — the specific pleasure is a channel that clearly means something and refuses to say what.

tail.title: I vibecoded a heavy-lift drone
tail.summary: A build log for a physically large drone where the flight-control and integration work was largely agent-written, including where that went badly. The interesting content is the failure boundary — which parts of a build with real torque and real crash costs the model could actually carry, and which it confidently could not.

tail.title: unslop.news: someone used AI to filter AI-focused content out of Hacker News
tail.summary: An HN mirror that classifies and strips AI content, built by someone who wanted the front page back. Structurally it is your news brief run in reverse — same source, same classification problem, inverted objective. Worth a look purely for how they handle the borderline cases, which is where your own fun-bucket filtering spends all its effort.

tail.title: open-notebook: a self-hosted NotebookLM with more control over the models
tail.summary: An open implementation of the source-grounded notebook pattern — drop in documents, ask questions, get answers with citations — but model-agnostic and running on your own machine. Directly comparable to the audio-overview and paper-library workflows you already have, with the difference that everything stays local and you choose the retrieval model.

tail.title: NotebookLM Calibre plugin
tail.summary: Pushes books from a Calibre library straight into NotebookLM notebooks. If your Calibre shelf holds the reference material behind the research or the novel, this removes the manual upload step between owning a book and being able to interrogate it.

tail.title: moonlit-stories: a reusable picture-book pipeline with consistent illustrations and local Chatterbox TTS
tail.summary: An end-to-end workflow that keeps character and style consistent across an illustrated book's pages and narrates it with a locally-run TTS model rather than a cloud voice. The consistency machinery is the transferable part — it is the same problem as keeping a character visually stable across a long-form project, solved with reference conditioning rather than luck.

tail.title: A handwriting simulator that turns plain text into convincing handwritten pages
tail.summary: Renders text as handwriting with letterpaper backgrounds and randomised perturbation of stroke, spacing and line height so it does not read as a font, with both a PyQt6 GUI and a CLI. Delightful and slightly alarming — the perturbation model is exactly what makes the output pass, and it is a nice concrete illustration of how little noise it takes to defeat 'looks generated'.

tail.title: An open-source video editor built for coding agents to drive
tail.summary: A programmable editor whose API surface is designed to be called by an agent rather than clicked by a person. Combined with the FFmpeg-plugin approach elsewhere this week, it is the emerging shape of agent-driven video: the model writes an edit decision list, the tool executes it deterministically.

tail.title: VoxWeave: a local-first offline RVC voice conversion workstation
tail.summary: Retrieval-based voice conversion with training and inference entirely offline, packaged as a workstation rather than a notebook. It is the audio analogue of what mimesis does with text — a model of one specific voice, fitted from that voice's own corpus — and the same consent and provenance questions apply, which makes it worth understanding rather than just noting.

tail.title: Claude Fleet: an always-on-top Claude Code session manager for Windows
tail.summary: A small floating widget showing the state of every running Claude Code session, built for Windows rather than macOS, which is unusual in this category. If you routinely have several agent sessions in flight — which a six-collector nightly run guarantees — this is the missing at-a-glance view of which ones are blocked.

tail.title: A Claude Code and Codex usage screen for the TRMNL e-ink display
tail.summary: Pushes live token and session usage for both agents to a low-power e-ink panel on your desk. Ambient rather than interactive, which is the right register for a number you want to notice but not check — and a cheap hardware project if you want your eval spend visible without a browser tab.

tail.title: Parley: let your coding agent talk to a teammate's agent
tail.summary: A message channel between agents running on different people's machines, so one agent can ask another for context rather than routing through the humans. Early and slightly unnerving, but it is the first credible answer to the question your multi-agent eval teardown raised — what happens when the coordination failure is between organisations rather than inside one harness.

tail.title: Turn any topic into a 60-second three-host AI podcast, no signup
tail.summary: A one-click generator for short multi-voice audio explainers.
