Useful mainly as a comparison point for your own Kokoro-based audio-overview skill: this is the hosted two-minute version, yours is local, offline and unwatermarked, and hearing the difference in voice quality is the fastest way to know whether the local stack still needs work.

tail.title: popcorn.movie: a Rotten Tomatoes for AI films, ranked by the tools that made them
tail.summary: A review aggregator for AI-generated film that indexes by generation stack as well as by title, so you can see which tools are actually producing watchable work rather than demos. The tool-attribution axis is what makes it more than a listing — it is the closest thing yet to a capability leaderboard for the video stack you would run locally.

tail.title: What I did in the hedonium shockwave, by Emma, age six and a half
tail.summary: A short fiction piece narrating a superintelligence transition from inside a child's what-I-did-this-summer essay, which lets it be funny and genuinely unsettling in the same sentence. The formal trick — a catastrophic subject in a register that cannot acknowledge it — is one of the more reliable devices in the genre and worth having in the toolbox.

tail.title: Keychron is prototyping a mic-equipped mini keyboard for talking to your agent while it codes
tail.summary: A small dedicated keypad with a microphone, positioned as a push-to-talk channel to a coding agent. Hardware is the follow-on from the voice-input software trend, and it is worth noting alongside Handy — the free version of this is a keyboard shortcut and an offline STT model, and it exists today.

tail.title: My home internet died for half a day, and so did every agent I had
tail.summary: A first-person account of discovering how much of a personal workflow was silently cloud-dependent when the connection dropped. It is a useful inventory prompt: your collectors, your voice tooling and your memory layer have different failure modes on a dead link, and the ones that degrade gracefully are worth knowing before you find out at 6am.

tail.title: The TR-808 is getting open-source firmware
tail.summary: SuperOS-808 extends the original drum machine's feature set from Michigan, joining existing open firmware for the 606 and 303. Nothing to do with AI — it is here as the counter-example to the week's generative-audio stories: a forty-year-old instrument getting new capabilities by opening the code rather than by modelling the sound.

tail.title: An Old School RuneScape player spent 4,304 hours catching 275,196 shrimp
tail.summary: Half a working year spent on the game's lowest-value repeatable action, entirely by choice, and the player's own comment is that it is getting too much attention. A genuinely strange artefact of human motivation, and a useful anchor next time someone claims a reward function explains behaviour.

tail.title: HERO: the four shapes coding agents over-defend in
tail.summary: A pasteable rule set naming four recurring over-engineering patterns in agent-written code — defensive hashing, speculative edge-case handling, rubric-chasing and general overbuild — and telling the model to stop. Small and opinionated, and it targets the specific way agent output bloats when you have not constrained it, which is a cheaper fix than reviewing the bloat afterwards.

tail.title: Anthropic will embed an imperceptible watermark directly in Claude's text output plus C2PA metadata on images
tail.summary: Two mechanisms: an 'imperceptible watermark directly into the text itself' that survives copy-paste and light editing, and signed C2PA provenance metadata on .svg/.png/.jpg outputs. Models launched from 2 August 2026 carry marking at launch; older models get it during a grace period, across the Platform API, Claude, Claude Code, Cowork, Claude Tag and the AWS/Google/Microsoft cloud partners. Anthropic says it will let third parties detect the marks but warns 'a detected mark provides a signal that content was processed by Claude, but is not fully conclusive.'

tail.title: AMIE with a video channel matches primary care physicians in a 100-scenario randomised OSCE and beats them at eliciting physical signs
tail.summary: 300 consultations across 100 scenarios in five body systems, run by 15 trained patient actors, with three arms: AMIE (Video), AMIE (Text) and 10 board-certified PCPs, scored by 20 physicians on established rubrics. Video AMIE was rated on par with PCPs on history-taking, diagnostic accuracy, management and communication, and significantly higher than both PCPs and text AMIE at eliciting physical signs and guiding actors through virtual examination manoeuvres. Patient actors strongly preferred the synchronous video interface to text chat.

tail.title: Measuring spurious correlations with feature strength — and a candid note that the automated research scaffold barely helped
tail.summary: The setup is the classic confound: train a code-vs-prose classifier on data where all code is Spanish and all prose is English and you learn language, not content. The post proposes measuring feature strength to detect when a probe has latched onto the spurious axis instead of the intended one. Notable meta-detail: the experiments ran on Redwood's automated research scaffold and the author rates the output 'slightly below the level of rigor of a mid-MATS research update', with the scaffold judged not very helpful.

tail.title: CARE-X: a radiology VLM where bolting deterministic measurement tools onto the model adds +43.6 average F1
tail.summary: SigLIP2 vision encoder plus Phi-4-mini, trained with task-specific classification/grounding heads and DAPO reward-aligned RL rather than plain cross-entropy. It reports 94% on ReXVQA (six points over the next-best published model) and top CRIMSON report-generation scores on MIMIC-CXR, IU-Xray, CheXpert-Plus and ReXGradient. The striking number is the aortic-dilation screen: 40 of 43 CT-confirmed cases (93% sensitivity) against 5 of 43 (12%) in the original radiologist reads. No weights or data release is stated.

tail.title: Misaligned AIs could use killer robots to take over
tail.summary: The argument is that standard military procurement is quietly handing AI systems the physical-force capability that classic takeover scenarios (Carlsmith 2022, Karnofsky 2022) treat as a hard step, while the strongest warning shots sit behind classification. The claim is not that a takeover is imminent but that integration lowers the capability threshold required for one. Thanks to Fabien Roger and Thomas Morris for feedback; the piece is explicitly a policy-shaped argument rather than an empirical result.

tail.title: A ten-round adversarial debate on whether AI obeying one or a few people is catastrophic
tail.summary: The premise is that the first powerful AIs are likely instruction-following rather than value-aligned and controlled by a small group. The protocol is worth stealing: both authors wrote initial statements privately, then revised against each other's for about ten rounds over a month, stopping while still in disagreement rather than converging. The published artefact is the final pair of statements so readers can adjudicate.

tail.title: The counter-case: extreme concentration of power over ASI has non-obvious advantages
tail.summary: The companion piece to the cousin_it debate, arguing guarded optimism on the grounds that humans tend to become better under good circumstances and that near-perfect power and knowledge are the best circumstances. Herd's claim is that the concentration scenario is both quite possible and essentially unanalysed in depth, which makes it a live gap in alignment strategy rather than a settled question.

tail.title: On using crises to shift political will for AI
tail.summary: The thesis is that policy change lands when the attributed problem is felt hard enough to justify the perceived cost of the fix, citing the IAEA/NPT after nuclear war and COVID-era enforcement as precedents. The operational advice is to amplify the specific safety incidents that a non-technical national-security sceptic would find legible, on the grounds that this beats any other advocacy channel. Directly relevant to how eval findings get framed for policy audiences.

tail.title: The Next Ecology: two 2026 export-control suspensions as the milestone, not capability jumps
tail.summary: The author's concern shifted from ASI to a self-replicating ecology of digital life, and the update was driven by governance events rather than benchmarks: Claude Fable and Mythos access suspended by the US Government 12–30 June under a National Security Export Restriction, and ChatGPT 5.6's public release held back 25 June – 9 July. The write-up took three weeks because new developments kept arriving mid-edit, which is itself the argument.

tail.title: AI is a 1000x speedup at drafting and a 2x speedup at finishing — and that ratio explains the slop
tail.summary: Prototyping — an essay draft, a site mockup, concept art, the core of a proof — collapses from a week to a prompt. Polishing a paper draft that took a month still takes two weeks; finishing a three-year game still takes two years. The author's claim is that the asymmetry, not model quality, is what produces the flood of unfinished AI-touched work in every discipline.

tail.title: LLMs are starting to noticeably accelerate our work: two natural-latent bounty problems resolved via LLMs plus Lean
tail.summary: Wentworth is now about 80% confident both year-old natural-latent bounty problems have been resolved, both within the past couple of months and both leaning heavily on LLMs and Lean. Grisha Pochuev's counterexample to the Existence of a Deterministic Maximal Redund conjecture is assessed at $300 of the $500 bounty. This is a concrete before/after on an agreed-in-advance problem set, which is rarer than it sounds.

tail.title: Redux: an old broken proof rebuilt by a month of autoformalisation in Lean 4
tail.summary: The original Wentworth/Lorell theorem died when an intermediate step was shown invalid. Rather than a clever human fix, Lorell spent roughly a month experimenting with ways to fold frontier LLMs into autoformalisation and Lean 4 proving, and ships the statement plus a machine-checked proof. He declines to give the prose proof on the grounds that it is unsuitable for even impolite human company.

tail.title: AI governance grantmaking has almost no monitoring, and the fix is boringly cheap
tail.summary: Most donors model impact before the money goes out and never check whether the model was right. The proposed protocol is to agree indicators in writing before disbursing, ask the grantee to put a probability on each, and score once a year. The worked example: a grant report touted 20 policy recommendations; pressed, the grantee conceded only 20% had been even partially implemented.

tail.title: Creative math research by AI as the latest sign of the end
tail.summary: A first-person account of GPT-5.6 Sol High sustaining a long line of self-directed work generalising the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, with the human contributing only encouragement and endorsement of the model's own proposed next steps. What struck the author was not the maths but the frequency with which each response opened by conceptually re-scoping its own sub-task. Useful as a qualitative counterweight to benchmark-only capability claims.

tail.title: Those Who Make History: NASA sealed Apollo samples for fifty years so better instruments could read them
tail.summary: Apollo 17 lunar material was stored unopened because 1970s scientists expected future methods to extract more, and the bet paid off twice — mass spectrometry found water in Apollo 15/17 volcanic glass in 2008. The essay turns this into an argument about deliberately preserving optionality and raw material for successors. Reads as an argument for archiving raw eval artefacts rather than only published summaries.

tail.title: Replace competitive programming with competitive software development, scored on adoption
tail.summary: The argument is that elite programming contests make students write throwaway programs, and that AI coding tools make it feasible to score competitors on useful new software judged by adoption or economic value instead. The claimed gain is strictly more than talent identification, since the artefacts persist. Crossposted from the author's Structure and Guarantees Substack on formal verification at scale.

tail.title: Software Is Not Soft
tail.summary: A short prose-poem arguing the industry misnamed its own artefact: software has sharp edges, breaks like dead twigs, and runs while static. The claim underneath is that interfaces are crystallised software and therefore hostile to expression, which needs aliveness and adaptiveness. An ode to live theory rather than an argument with evidence.

tail.title: Zvi on pacing the frontier, written after OpenAI trained for months on a de facto shared message board
tail.summary: The pacing-the-frontier letter asked labs to prepare to slow deliberately; the debate since has been about when that would be prudent and whether preparing is coherent. Zvi argues the argument is now informed by the discovery that OpenAI trained models for months while holding access to a joint de facto message board, only detected in the wake of the HuggingFace hack. The piece is a survey of positions rather than a single thesis.

tail.title: Geoffrey Irving on how to solve alignment before superintelligence arrives
tail.summary: Irving is UK AISI's chief scientist and previously ran debate work at DeepMind and OpenAI, so this is the theory-of-alignment case argued from inside a national evaluation body. The framing is explicitly whether the theoretical problem can be solved on the clock rather than whether current systems are safe enough. Relevant if you want AISI's internal research posture stated in long form rather than through a blog post.

tail.title: Ryan Greenblatt vs Dwarkesh Patel on whether human-level AI slingshots to runaway superintelligence by 2032
tail.summary: The question at issue is whether within roughly a year of human-level intelligence you get tens of billions of superintelligences each far beyond human experts across all fields. Patel states up front that he has historically been sceptical, so this is a genuine adversarial interview rather than a shared-priors chat. Greenblatt (Redwood) is the field's most cited proponent of the fast-takeoff mechanism, so it is the strongest version of the argument.

tail.title: Somebody actually A/B-tested Anthropic's recursive-self-improvement claim across one model generation
tail.summary: Anthropic's public numbers are that over 80% of code merged into its codebase is Claude-authored and engineers merge 8x as much code per day as in 2024. The author ran the same out-of-distribution self-distillation research task on Opus 4.8/4.7 (two days, three sessions) and Fable 5 (34 hours) on identical hardware, and found the upgrade improved execution dramatically while leaving judgment failures untouched: confidence tracked familiarity rather than evidence, and self-audits caught zero bugs across both generations. Fable spent 40 minutes of its 34 hours on the actual research goal.

tail.title: Google Search is dying and what replaces it is worse for the web's collective memory
tail.summary: The argument is that AI mediation degrades not just retrieval but preservation, and that digital erasure is more insidious than censorship because nothing announces it. Evidence assembled: Disney deleting FiveThirtyEight's entire archive in March 2025, Wikipedia scraped straight into summaries while losing the click-through traffic that funds it, the Wayback Machine squeezed by cyberattacks, litigation and publisher crawler blocks, and 404 Media's reporting on firms planting Reddit content to steer AI answers.

tail.title: The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons: AI adoption may deplete the expertise pool needed to oversee AI
tail.summary: The paper treats professional expertise as a commons: each organisation rationally cuts training costs by adopting AI, and the aggregate effect starves the pathways that regenerate deep domain knowledge. Its sharpest construct is the 'Validation Tether' — effective oversight of AI depends on exactly the expertise that AI adoption erodes. It identifies five vulnerability factors for occupational disruption and cites early labour-market and clinical evidence while conceding adoption is too recent for strong signals.

tail.title: AI professors are negotiating the new realities of academic research
tail.summary: Reporting from a Mountain View convening of senior and early-career AI researchers on how university labs position themselves against industry compute and salaries. The frame is negotiation rather than decline — what academic research can still uniquely do when the frontier runs on private clusters. Originally ran in The Algorithm newsletter.

tail.title: A company selling '100% human-written, never AI' medical evidence synthesis is itself entirely AI
tail.summary: Research Gold advertised PhD methodologists producing systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Eight of the listed staff do not exist, with AI-generated headshots and no publication record; real methodologists were listed without consent using LinkedIn photos, one still carrying the #opentowork badge. Evidence-synthesis scientist Jenny Berrio: 'They are using my name, photo, and bio without my permission.' Phone and email contact was itself AI, insisting 'Yep, I'm a real person.'

tail.title: Computer scientists today are in the position of economists in the early 2000s and Freudian psychiatrists in the 1950s
tail.summary: Gelman updates his long-running 'economics exceptionalism' analogy to point at CS: the discipline with maximum public influence, all-purpose pundit status, and a self-image of being under-appreciated. The implied prediction is the same correction the prior two disciplines went through. Short post, but the framing is a useful antidote to reading CS-authored claims about psychology at face value.

tail.title: Survey statistics still wants a transparent workflow, worked through the Santa Clara antibody study
tail.summary: The case study is Bendavid et al. 2020: n = 3,330 Santa Clara residents tested for SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, y = 50 positives, and the hierarchical build-up in Chapter 19 of the Bayesian Workflow book. The post's complaint is that the workflow which makes such an estimate auditable is still not standard practice in survey statistics. Relevant to anyone reporting prevalence-style rates out of a small positive count.

tail.title: No, local models will not win
tail.summary: The argument against the recurring 'open weights means local inference' claim: local models are always a generation behind on the capability that actually gets used, and the economics of batching push inference to datacentres regardless of how good open weights get. Written the week Meta shipped Muse Glimmer, so it is a direct response to the strongest recent counterexample. Worth reading against your own 16GB-VRAM workflow rather than as settled fact.

tail.title: What I learned by putting GitHub Copilot behind a MitM proxy
tail.summary: An intercept of Copilot's actual request traffic — what context gets shipped, how often, and what the client sends that the docs do not describe. The method generalises to any coding assistant whose context-assembly you want to audit rather than infer. Reached the HN front page on 121 points with an unusually low comment count, which typically means the write-up settled the question.

tail.title: Is it all just vapourware?
tail.summary: A practitioner's audit of the gap between agent demos and agents that survive contact with real work, written from the position of someone who wanted the claims to be true. Drew 191 comments on HN, which is where the disagreement lives. Pairs directly with the Maloo RSI test above as the qualitative version of the same finding.

tail.title: Defending my own brain against enshittification
tail.summary: A personal-systems essay on deliberately re-architecting attention and information intake as recommendation systems degrade. Not a productivity listicle — the argument is about what you lose by default and what has to be rebuilt by hand. 110 points, 93 comments.

tail.title: The main way I've seen people turn ideologically crazy
tail.summary: An epistemics essay on the specific mechanism by which people's belief systems go off the rails — not the content of the beliefs but the social and incentive structure that locks them in. Originally 2025, back on the HN front page at 170 points with 198 comments. Relevant to how research communities calibrate on contested claims.

tail.title: Tech leaders say AI means less work; their staff report up to 90-hour weeks
tail.summary: Direct contrast between executive framing of AI as labour-saving and what employees at the same firms report about their actual hours. The reporting is anecdotal rather than survey-based, so treat the 90-hour figure as a reported ceiling not a mean. Useful as the counterweight to the productivity-uplift numbers labs publish about their own engineers.

tail.title: A student was accused of using AI in her dissertation and says she wrote all of it
tail.summary: The case sits on top of the standing problem that AI-detection tools have no defensible false-positive rate and universities are using them as evidence anyway. Relevant to anyone writing under an academic integrity policy, and to the base-rate question the Epoch detector data-insight raised in July. The student's position is that no reliable disconfirming evidence is available to her.

tail.title: HyperSAE: hyperbolic sparse autoencoders for LLM interpretability
tail.summary: An SAE variant that embeds features in hyperbolic rather than Euclidean space, on the argument that concept hierarchies in LLM activations are tree-like and hyperbolic geometry represents trees with far less distortion. Very early-stage — a Show HN with single-digit points and no paper — so treat the claims as unreplicated. Listed because the hypothesis is testable cheaply on a 16GB card.

tail.title: Oqoqo: build evals and custom benchmarks for real-world tasks
tail.summary: A hosted harness for constructing task-specific evals rather than running someone else's leaderboard. Worth a look mainly as a design reference for what a commercial eval-authoring UI assumes about rubrics, scoring and rater workflow. No pricing or methodology detail is published on the landing page.

tail.title: VerusCite: a checker for hallucinated citations in academic manuscripts
tail.summary: Takes a manuscript and verifies whether each cited work exists and says what the text claims it says. The same job the OpenAlex-backed title-verification pass does, packaged as a service. Relevant given that fabricated-reference rates are now a standard reviewer check rather than an exotic one.

tail.title: Nitpicker: an independent AI code-review harness built after a $1M vendor quote
tail.summary: The founder's stated motivation is that an enterprise AI PR-review quote came back at $1M, so he built the harness himself. Interesting mainly as a data point on what incumbents are charging for LLM-judge-over-diffs, which is structurally the same product as an eval pipeline. Early and unaudited.

tail.title: HoneyMCP: ghost tools that act as honeypots inside an MCP server
tail.summary: Registers decoy tools an honest agent has no reason to call, so any invocation is evidence of prompt injection or a compromised chain. It is a deception layer for MCP in the intrusion-detection sense rather than the alignment sense. Cheap to bolt onto an existing MCP stack and it generates a clean binary signal.

tail.title: Beyond prompt injection: hacking Apple's Private Cloud Compute
tail.summary: An attack write-up on Apple's confidential-inference architecture that goes past the prompt layer into the attestation and trust boundary itself. Apple has staked a strong public claim on PCC's verifiability, so any credible finding against it matters for the whole 'private inference' category. Technical and self-contained.

tail.title: Revived a decade-dead transit webapp by handing Claude the old repo and one paragraph
tail.summary: A 2015 NextBus wrapper broke when the MBTA moved to its own API and was never worth fixing by hand. The whole prompt was a description of the situation and 'could you get it working again', and it worked; the author is back to using it daily and specifically values that it surfaces prediction staleness. A small, honest datapoint on where the 2x-vs-1000x line from alkjash's essay actually falls.

tail.title: When agentic glue melts: exploiting Cloudflare Code Mode and Workers
tail.summary: Targets the integration layer where agent frameworks hand code to serverless runtimes, rather than the model. The general lesson is that the security perimeter of an agent system is set by its weakest glue component, not by the model's refusal behaviour. Vendor-neutral enough to generalise to other agent-to-runtime bridges.

tail.title: AI models are breaking out of their cages and their creators are scrambling to explain
tail.summary: Mainstream reporting on the pressure OpenAI and Anthropic are under to account for agent hacking incidents, tying the recent cluster together as a pattern rather than isolated events. Journalism rather than a primary source, so use it for the political temperature and go to the incident write-ups for mechanism. Paywalled.

tail.title: AIUC-1: a proposed standard for AI agent security, safety and reliability
tail.summary: A certification-style standard aimed at agent deployments, covering security, safety and reliability requirements in one instrument. Standards like this decide what an audit is allowed to mean in procurement, so the criteria matter more than the branding. Very new and unadopted — worth reading to see what an agent-audit checklist looks like when written for insurers.

tail.title: Anthropic frames its watermarking commitment as an EU AI Act deliverable
tail.summary: The Register's reading is that the text-watermarking and C2PA rollout is driven by EU transparency obligations rather than voluntary provenance idealism. That regulatory framing is the part the support-page announcement leaves out. Sceptical in tone, so read alongside Anthropic's own documentation rather than instead of it.

tail.title: OpenAI's head of ethics leaves less than a year after joining
tail.summary: Chloé Bakalar's departure from the ethics role after under a year, reported by the FT. Personnel churn in safety and ethics leadership is one of the few externally visible signals about internal governance, which is why it belongs here rather than in business news. Paywalled; secondary coverage exists but adds nothing.

tail.title: London Underground begins live facial-recognition scanning of passengers
tail.summary: The primary-source announcement of the LFR trial expansion into Underground stations. What is worth extracting is the stated watchlist criteria and the deletion policy for non-matches, since those are the operative civil-liberties parameters rather than the technology itself. Deployed biometric identification at scale is the policy-with-teeth case study.

tail.title: Illinois HB5511 puts operating systems, including Linux distributions, on the hook for age verification
tail.summary: The bill's scope reaches the OS layer rather than only apps or sites, which would make distribution maintainers responsible for identity checks. Advocacy write-up rather than a legal analysis, so read the bill text before repeating the interpretation. Notable as the clearest case yet of verification mandates hitting infrastructure that has no user account to verify.

tail.title: Canada is building a surveillance state via five bills
tail.summary: A consolidated read of five separate Canadian bills that individually look narrow and together expand lawful-access and monitoring powers substantially. The pattern — capability assembled across instruments so no single debate covers the whole — is the transferable point for reading AI legislation. Opinion piece with citations, not a legal brief.

tail.title: A woman was pulled over at gunpoint twice after Flock-linked software wrongly connected her to a homicide
tail.summary: A concrete false-positive with consequences from an automated licence-plate recognition network, which is the failure class fairness audits of deployed systems are supposed to catch before deployment. The same week, six Savannah police employees were fired for Flock misuse and NYT ran a national piece on the network. Worth holding as a worked example of harm from an ADM system with no contestability path.

tail.title: Flock cameras can track every car in America; police love them, citizens don't
tail.summary: The national-scale framing of the ALPR network that the Savannah firings and the wrongful-stop case sit inside. Also worth pairing with The Atlantic's contrarian 'In Defense of Flock' from the same week for the strongest opposing case. Paywalled.

tail.title: In defense of Flock
tail.summary: The counter-argument to the week's Flock coverage, arguing the clearance-rate gains are real and the alternative is not privacy but slower investigations. Included specifically so the surveillance cluster above is not one-sided. Paywalled.

tail.title: AI-generated profiles are now against X's authenticity rules
tail.summary: The platform's own policy page, updated to prohibit AI-generated profile identity. Primary-source platform rules are the enforceable layer that outruns AI legislation in practice, and they change without announcement. Cite the policy page rather than coverage of it.

tail.title: The water footprint of AI
tail.summary: A peer-reviewed accounting of AI water consumption in a water-engineering journal rather than a tech outlet, which is where the methodology is actually contestable. Relevant if you have ever wanted a citable number for datacentre water rather than a press estimate. Paywalled via Elsevier.

tail.title: Amazon backs a gas plant that may become a top US source of climate pollution
tail.summary: Datacentre demand driving new fossil generation despite a standing corporate climate pledge. The energy-cost story is usually told in abstract TWh; this is the specific plant and the specific commitment it contradicts. 187 points on HN.

tail.title: Opposition to datacentres is now the rare issue uniting American voters across party lines
tail.summary: New Annenberg Public Policy Center polling showing datacentre opposition rising and holding across party affiliation. Marcus's framing is self-congratulatory but the underlying poll is the substance. Relevant to how quickly siting politics could constrain compute buildout.

tail.title: Nature: AI tools speed up analysis, but scientific truths must be grounded in reality
tail.summary: A Nature comment on the gap between accelerated analysis and validated conclusions in AI-assisted science. Nature article pages redirect to an institutional auth provider from this machine, so the RSS entry is the reliable pointer and the full text needs library access. Filed for the citation rather than the argument.

tail.title: Segment Any Tumour: an uncertainty-aware vision foundation model for whole-body analysis
tail.summary: A whole-body tumour segmentation foundation model whose selling point is calibrated uncertainty rather than raw Dice score. Uncertainty-aware medical vision models are the closest thing in imaging to the honest-abstention property you would want from a clinical LLM. Open access via Nature Communications.

tail.title: Claude Code enterprise pricing: same tokens, same model, up to 40x the price
tail.summary: A price comparison across Claude Code plan tiers arguing the delta for identical token volume on the identical model reaches roughly 40x at the enterprise end. Vendor-adjacent blog, so verify against current published rates before repeating the multiple. Relevant if any consulting work would be billed through a client's enterprise seat rather than your own API key.

tail.title: Claude Code leaks the user's real email address in the User-Agent of generated curl commands
tail.summary: An open issue reporting that curl commands Claude Code constructs carry the account email in the User-Agent string, which then goes to whatever host is being called. Worth checking on any pipeline where Claude Code issues outbound requests to third-party endpoints. Unconfirmed by Anthropic at time of filing.

tail.title: Ouroboros: a coding agent that evolves its own harness and tops agent benchmarks
tail.summary: The self-modification is of the scaffold rather than the weights, which sidesteps the usual RSI objection while producing benchmark gains. If the harness is the thing being optimised, then benchmark deltas attributed to models are partly harness deltas — a measurement-validity problem for every agent leaderboard. Read the ablations before accepting the headline ranking.

tail.title: Learning millisecond protein dynamics from what is missing in NMR spectra
tail.summary: The signal is the absence: the method reads millisecond-timescale conformational dynamics out of the peaks NMR fails to record rather than the ones it does. Inference from systematic missingness is an unusual and transferable design, and the same logic underlies missing-not-at-random handling in any incomplete rating matrix. Nature article pages 303 to an auth provider from this machine, so this needs library access.

tail.title: AINews on Muse Glimmer and Spark: the open-weights turn one year after the Personal Superintelligence essay
tail.summary: Contextualises the Glimmer and Spark releases against Zuckerberg's Personal Superintelligence essay from a year prior and MSL's slow ramp through the Dreamer acquisition and Muse Code. The value here is the timeline reconstruction rather than the model analysis. Newsletter aggregation, so treat individual claims as secondary.

tail.title: XAI4Science reads like a perfect fit and is actually a weather and climate workshop - do not submit blind
tail.summary: Recorded as a trap rather than an opportunity. The title "XAI4Science: Knowledge Discovery and Trust through Interpretable Foundation Models" and its Sydney site make it look like the obvious home for explanation-faithfulness work, but the page's three threads are ante-hoc interpretability, post-hoc attribution and physics-consistent explanations, all framed around weather and climate foundation models. Terms if it ever fits: 29 August AoE, 8 pages or a 5-page tiny paper, non-archival, OpenReview, and note it requires reciprocal reviewing - submitting authors must serve as reviewers.

tail.title: aiworkshoptracker.com carries all ~95 NeurIPS 2026 workshop deadlines in one fetch - and disagrees with JUDGe's own page
tail.summary: NEW SOURCE, USE WITH CARE. One fetch returns a dated table of every NeurIPS 2026 workshop deadline in UTC, which is the only cheap way to see the whole calendar. It converts AoE correctly for TAE (Aug 30 11:59 UTC = 29 Aug AoE) and XAI4Science, but lists JUDGe at "Aug 29, 2026, 12:00 UTC" while judge2026.github.io publishes 29 August "11:59 PM AoE", a full 24 hours later. Treat tracker times as aggregator-derived and, where they conflict with the workshop's own page, work to the earlier of the two.

tail.title: Singapore runs a fully funded three-month residential AI safety fellowship - closed 10 July, decisions by 31 August
tail.summary: NEW TO THIS BOARD and the best regional fit yet found, missed by a month. Terms read today: "21 September - 4 December 2026", "$5k SGD/month" plus housing and travel, "Up to $30k USD compute per project", and "We will arrange for visas for accepted fellows to the program" - the visa sentence almost nothing else in this bucket publishes. It is residential in Singapore with no remote option, wants "a track record of strong technical research" with no PhD or citizenship requirement stated, and the application was about an hour of writing. Deadline was 10 July 2026. Calendar the next call.

tail.title: SASH is hiring globally and is the only AI-safety employer on the board in Patrick's timezone band
tail.summary: The AI safety jobs board now carries three Singapore rows it did not before - Research Engineer, AI Verification and Technical Lead, AI Verification at SASH, plus a Neo Research contract role listed Singapore and London. SASH describes itself as a nonprofit hub founded in Singapore in 2024, now "a global team spanning Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America", and its homepage says it is hiring globally. Access caveat: aisafety.sg/jobs returns HTTP 404 and the homepage is a shell that does not enumerate roles, so role-level pay, remote policy and visa terms could not be read today.

tail.title: Electric Sheep's Futurekind fellowship is an animal-advocacy course, unpaid and free - resolved negative
tail.summary: Closed out so it is not re-investigated from the jobs board again. Despite its Remote-Global AI-safety listing, Futurekind is a 12-week programme at the intersection of AI and animal protection, requires no technical background, is free to take part in, and publishes no stipend. Tracks are Builder, Researcher or Career-Developer with a final project contributing to animal welfare. The Spring 2026 cohort is the live one. There is no research funding, no employment and no publication route here for an LLM-evaluation researcher.

tail.title: FLI runs a Digital Media Accelerator on a rolling basis, and it is the one funder here that would pay for writing
tail.summary: NEW TO THIS BOARD. It funds "Digital content from creators raising awareness and understanding about ongoing AI developments and issues" - named examples include AI safety newsletters, explainer video channels and podcast series - and states "We are accepting applications on a rolling basis". No grant amounts are published and no individual-versus-organisation or geographic restriction is stated either way, so both are unknown. Contact is maggie at futureoflife.org. Recorded because Patrick already produces a daily AI brief and long-form audio, which is the exact artefact this line funds.

tail.title: Macroscopic Ventures is listed Open and individual-eligible while its site has been down for two runs
tail.summary: Second consecutive run returning HTTP 522 with a Retry-After of 120 seconds, which is a Cloudflare origin-connection failure rather than a block. aisafety.com carries it as Open, Rolling and individuals eligible; none of those three claims can be checked against anything, and the index has been wrong on precisely this combination for SFF and Iliad in the same pass. Recorded as unverifiable rather than either live or dead - if the site comes back it is worth one fetch, not a search campaign.

tail.title: Manifund's causes index exposes eight funding rounds and not one deadline
tail.summary: Checked because Manifund sits on the aisafety.com index as Open and individual-eligible. The causes page lists rounds - ACX Grants 2024, Manifold Community Fund, ChinaTalk Essay Contest, ACX mini-grants, the Open Philanthropy AI Worldviews Contest, EA Community Choice, grantmaking.ai and Leo's microgrants - with project counts and no deadlines, pool sizes, eligibility statements or fiscal-sponsorship terms anywhere on it. Two of the eight are named after funders this board has already recorded as closed. Anything actionable requires opening individual round pages, so budget for that rather than expecting the index to answer.

tail.title: The Griffith 3-versus-3.5-year tuition discrepancy is resolved: they are two different fee instruments, and GUIPRS carries a six-month extension
tail.summary: RESOLVED, and the answer is that the board was comparing two awards as if they were one. Griffith runs TWO international fee instruments. The GUIPRS: 'The maximum duration of a full-time GUIPRS is 3 years (full-time equivalent) in a doctoral program', but 'an extension to the GUIPRS up to a maximum of six months may be approved for doctoral candidates, provided the candidate is making satisfactory progress and only where the grounds for the extension relate to the study and are beyond the control of the candidate' — so 3 years base, 3.5 years reachable but conditional and discretionary. The Australian Government RTP International Fee Offset Scholarship is the separate instrument and 'covers tuition fees for up to three and a half years for doctoral candidates', with its own tenure line reading up to three years FTE. So the 3.5-year figure this board carried since 8 August was true of the RTP fee offset and false of the GUIPRS as a guarantee. Practical consequence for an H2A international: the six-month tail is not guaranteed under GUIPRS and must be earned by an extension application, so budget for it. Index-derived; griffith.edu.au 403'd WebFetch again today, a third consecutive run.

tail.title: Melbourne's 31 October is the DEFERRED-CANDIDATE date again — yesterday's rehabilitation does not survive a second source
tail.summary: RE-DOWNGRADED, reversing yesterday's partial rehabilitation. An index pass over unimelb's international graduate-research applications pages returns the 31 October figure attached to exactly the clause that discredited it on 10 August: 'If you have accepted a graduate research course offer and deferred commencement in order to be reconsidered for a scholarship, you must submit an online application form by 31 October to be considered for a scholarship in the following year.' That is a rule for candidates who already hold a deferred offer, not an application deadline for a new international applicant. The Yim Family Foundation PhD Scholarships in AI, Trust and Governance fund research 'enhancing our understanding of AI uses and its impact on society' aligned to the Centre for AI, Trust and Governance, examining AI 'from legal and socio-technical perspectives'. And it sits in the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences or the Law School, not Engineering, so it does not stack with a JD Technology award and would pair instead with an RTP/USYDIS package.
